>> the AI can't build new theory yet, but can do insane brute-force, which turns out to be surprisingly powerful, and probably the theory building will get there eventually

A lot of cutting edge math is close to brute-force search, like to throwing stuff to the wall to see what sticks. But at the high level instead of throwing bolts and nuts, you throw BMW and Ferrari.

For example, it's very hard to know how hard a problem is when you already know the solution. It's much easier to verify that the solution is correct than imagining how hard is guessing the tricks to solve it.

Usually after a big proof, parts are reused by the community to prove similar stuff and followups. After a while, the tricks get a name, perhaps lemas are upgraded to theorems, and they may get their own book or course. It's similar to refactoring in programming.

From Andrew Wiles:

> Perhaps I could best describe my experience of doing mathematics in terms of entering a dark mansion. You go into the first room and it's dark, completely dark. You stumble around, bumping into the furniture. Gradually, you learn where each piece of furniture is. And finally, after six months or so, you find the light switch and turn it on. Suddenly, it's all illuminated and you can see exactly where you were. Then you enter the next dark room...

Could someone explain the difference (if any) between the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and what has historically been called the Riemann Hypothesis?

simonreiff · Nov 21, 2026

The Riemann hypothesis is a statement about the nontrivial complex-valued zeroes of the Riemann zeta function given by zeta(s) := sum to infinity of 1/n^s, namely that such zeroes all have real part 1/2. It has been extended and specialized many ways since being posed by Riemann over 150 years ago, but perhaps the most important is the generalized Riemann hypothesis which replaces the Riemann zeta function with the Dirichlet L-function. In other words GRH says: All nontrivial zeroes of the Dirichlet L-function L(chi, s) = sum to infinity of chi(n)/n^s, for primitive Dirichlet character chi, have real part 1/2.
